traditions.name: Rub Woolsey's Foot
traditions.description: Generations of students have rubbed the protruding foot of the bronze statue of President Theodore Dwight Woolsey on Old Campus for good luck. Visitors can give the shiny foot a rub too.

traditions.name: Hear the Harkness Carillon
traditions.description: Students in the Yale Guild of Carillonneurs play the carillon in Harkness Tower twice a day during the school year, at 12:30 and 5:30 p.m., plus Friday concerts in summer. Visitors can listen from the streets and courtyards nearby.

traditions.name: Visit the Women's Table
traditions.description: Maya Lin's 1993 Women's Table in front of Sterling Memorial Library is carved with a spiral of numbers showing how many women studied at Yale each year since 1701. Visitors can walk up and read the spiral.

details.airportInfo: Bradley, near Hartford, is about an hour's drive north of New Haven. Many visitors also fly into New York and take Metro-North's New Haven Line straight to Union Station.
details.funFact: Yale's central campus is the finest collection of Collegiate Gothic in America: most of it was designed by James Gamble Rogers in the 1920s and 1930s, with acid poured on the stone and windows deliberately cracked to make the new buildings look centuries old.
details.languageInfo: Campus life has its own vocabulary: undergraduates belong to one of fourteen residential colleges, and the bell tower everyone meets under is simply 'Harkness'.
details.transportationFact: The central campus is compact and best seen on foot. The free Yale Shuttle loops between the colleges, the Science Hill and the medical campus.

buildings.name: Sterling Memorial Library
buildings.description: Designed to look like a Gothic cathedral, Yale's main library has a nave, side aisles and a circulation desk where the altar would be. Its book tower holds millions of volumes behind the stained glass.

buildings.name: Harkness Tower
buildings.description: Yale's bell tower rises 66 metres over the Memorial Quadrangle, a masonry Gothic spire built between 1917 and 1921 in memory of Charles William Harkness. It now anchors Branford College and is the landmark everyone on campus navigates by.
buildings.address: Memorial Quadrangle (Branford College), New Haven, CT 06511

buildings.wiki: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library
buildings.name: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library
buildings.description: A windowless box of translucent Vermont marble, just 1.25 inches thick, so daylight seeps through the panels in a soft amber glow. Inside, a six-story glass tower of rare books stands at the heart of the building.

buildings.name: Yale University Art Gallery
buildings.description: The oldest university art museum in the Western Hemisphere. Its modernist main building, finished in 1953, was one of Louis Kahn's first works and the commission that transformed his career; it links to the older 1928 gallery and Gothic Street Hall.

buildings.name: Yale Center for British Art
buildings.description: Louis Kahn's last building, finished after his death and opened in 1977: matte steel and reflective glass outside, travertine, white oak and Belgian linen inside. Its galleries hold the largest collection of British art outside the United Kingdom in soft natural light.

buildings.name: David S. Ingalls Rink
buildings.description: Everyone calls Eero Saarinen's hockey rink 'The Whale' for its swooping humpbacked roof, hung on cables from a single arching concrete spine. Completed in 1958, it seats 3,500 fans under a ceiling 23 metres high.

buildings.name: Rudolph Hall
buildings.description: One of the earliest and best-known Brutalist buildings in America, Paul Rudolph's home for Yale's architecture school packs more than 30 floor levels into seven stories of ribbed, bush-hammered concrete.
buildings.address: Chapel St & York St, New Haven, CT 06511

traditions.name: Touch John Harvard's Left Foot
traditions.description: Touching the left foot of the John Harvard statue in Harvard Yard is said to bring good luck, and it has been polished to a golden shine. Guides call it the 'statue of three lies', and visitors often pose for a photo with it.

traditions.name: Read Both Sides of Dexter Gate
traditions.description: Dexter Gate on Massachusetts Avenue reads 'Enter to grow in wisdom' on the outside and 'Depart to serve better thy country and thy kind' on the inside. Visitors can walk through and read both inscriptions.

traditions.name: Sheriffs at Johnston Gate
traditions.description: For centuries, the sheriffs of Middlesex and Suffolk Counties have ridden into Harvard Yard on horseback on Commencement Day, traditionally through Johnston Gate. Visitors can see the 1889 gate, the Yard's main entrance, at any time.

details.airportInfo: Logan is about 8 km from Harvard Square across the harbour. The MBTA Silver Line and Red Line connect the airport to the Harvard stop.
details.funFact: Within a few minutes' walk of Harvard Yard you can see the college's oldest surviving building, Georgian Massachusetts Hall of 1720, and the only building in the United States designed primarily by Le Corbusier.
details.languageInfo: Students simply say 'the Yard' for Harvard Yard, the leafy heart of the campus where the oldest halls stand.
details.transportationFact: Harvard Yard and its neighbours are best explored on foot. The Red Line's Harvard station opens right onto Harvard Square, a short ride from downtown Boston.

buildings.name: Massachusetts Hall
buildings.description: Harvard's oldest surviving building, a plain brick Georgian hall raised between 1718 and 1720. Built as a dormitory for 64 students, it quartered 640 American soldiers during the Siege of Boston and now holds the president's office.

buildings.name: University Hall
buildings.description: Charles Bulfinch, one of America's first great architects, designed this crisp white granite hall, built in 1813–1815 from Chelmsford stone. It was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1970.

buildings.name: Memorial Hall
buildings.description: A towering High Victorian Gothic memorial to Harvard men who fought for the Union in the Civil War. Under one roof it holds Sanders Theatre, the great timbered dining hall now called Annenberg Hall, and a hushed memorial transept.
buildings.architect: William Robert Ware and Henry Van Brunt
buildings.address: North of Harvard Yard, Cambridge, MA 02138
buildings.oldUse: Civil War memorial and dining hall

buildings.name: Sever Hall
buildings.description: H. H. Richardson's mature masterpiece in Harvard Yard: a warm red-brick block of rounded arches and carved brickwork from the late 1870s. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1970.

buildings.name: Widener Library
buildings.description: Built by Eleanor Elkins Widener in memory of her son, lost on the Titanic, this colonnaded giant opened in 1915. A grand flight of steps leads to Corinthian columns, and behind them 57 miles of shelves wind through ten levels of stacks.

buildings.wiki: Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts
buildings.name: Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts
buildings.description: The only building in the United States designed primarily by Le Corbusier: a sculptural concrete home for the visual arts, designed with Guillermo Jullian de la Fuente in his Paris studio and completed in 1962.

traditions.name: MIThenge
traditions.description: On a few days around mid-November and late January, the setting sun lines up with the Infinite Corridor and shines down its whole length. Crowds gather in the corridor to watch the light pour through.

traditions.name: Smoot markers on the Harvard Bridge
traditions.description: The Harvard Bridge sidewalk is painted with marks measuring its length in 'smoots', the height of 1958 pledge Oliver Smoot. Walk the bridge to find the 'Halfway to Hell' mark and the final '364.4 smoots plus or minus one ear'.

details.airportInfo: Logan is about 7 km from MIT across the Charles River. The MBTA links the airport to Kendall/MIT station on the Red Line.
details.funFact: MIT names nearly all its buildings by number, so the Great Dome is Building 10 and Frank Gehry's Stata Center is Building 32, standing on the site of the legendary Building 20 that housed the wartime Radiation Laboratory.
details.languageInfo: At MIT you ask for directions by number: rooms are written like 'W16-100', building then room.
details.transportationFact: The campus runs along the Charles River and is easy to walk end to end. Kendall/MIT station on the Red Line sits at its eastern edge.

buildings.name: Stata Center
buildings.description: Frank Gehry's tumbling, tilting academic complex looks as if its towers are about to topple into each other. It opened in 2004 on the site of Building 20, which housed the historic wartime Radiation Laboratory.

buildings.name: Kresge Auditorium
buildings.description: Eero Saarinen's thin-shell concrete dome is one-eighth of a sphere, proportionately thinner than an eggshell, resting on just three points with glass curtain walls filling the gaps. It was dedicated in 1955.

buildings.name: MIT Chapel
buildings.description: From outside, a windowless brick cylinder in a shallow moat; inside, light rippling up from the water and a shimmering metal screen by Harry Bertoia falling from a skylight onto a plain marble altar. Saarinen designed it as a companion to Kresge Auditorium.

buildings.name: Green Building
buildings.description: I. M. Pei, an MIT graduate, designed this 18-story concrete tower for the earth sciences, one of the tallest buildings in Cambridge. It opened in 1964.
buildings.architect: I. M. Pei and Araldo Cossutta

traditions.name: FitzRandolph Gate superstition
traditions.description: Campus legend says students who walk out through FitzRandolph Gate before graduation will not finish their degree, so undergraduates avoid it until Commencement. Visitors can see the gate on Nassau Street and decide for themselves which way to walk.

traditions.name: Arch sings at Blair Arch
traditions.description: Blair Arch, the largest arch on campus, is where many of Princeton's a cappella 'arch sings' take place. Stop under the arch to hear its echo, or catch a free evening concert.

traditions.name: Big Cannon on Cannon Green
traditions.description: A Revolutionary-era cannon has been buried muzzle-down on Cannon Green behind Nassau Hall since 1840, and it is slowly sinking. Visitors can see the exposed end; the green is also where the bonfire is lit when Princeton beats both Harvard and Yale in football.

details.airportInfo: Newark is about an hour's drive north. NJ Transit trains run from the airport station to Princeton Junction, where the short shuttle train known as the Dinky continues to campus.
details.funFact: Nassau Hall was the largest academic building in the American colonies when it opened in 1756, and in 1783 it served as the United States Capitol for four months.
details.languageInfo: Nassau Hall is affectionately known as 'Old Nassau', a name that also belongs to the university's alma mater song.
details.transportationFact: The campus is compact and green, and best seen on foot. The Dinky shuttle train links Princeton station with Princeton Junction on the main New York–Philadelphia line.

buildings.name: Nassau Hall
buildings.description: Princeton's oldest building was the largest in colonial New Jersey when completed in 1756 and briefly served as the US Capitol in 1783. After fires it was rebuilt by Benjamin Latrobe and then John Notman, who added its cupola.
buildings.architect: Robert Smith; later Benjamin Latrobe and John Notman

buildings.name: Princeton University Chapel
buildings.description: Ralph Adams Cram's sandstone and limestone chapel evokes a small English cathedral, with a nave, transepts and four great stained-glass windows. When finished in 1928 its only rival in size among university chapels was King's College Chapel, Cambridge.

buildings.name: Firestone Library
buildings.description: Princeton's main library, the Harvey S. Firestone Memorial Library, opened in 1948 in Collegiate Gothic dress to match the campus. It is the headquarters of a system holding more than seven million books.
buildings.architect: Robert B. O'Connor and Walter H. Kilham Jr.

buildings.name: Alexander Hall
buildings.description: A rugged Richardsonian Romanesque hall finished in 1894, built to host commencement and now home to the 900-seat Richardson Auditorium and the Princeton Symphony Orchestra.

buildings.name: Prospect House
buildings.description: John Notman's sandstone villa of 1851, with its three-story tower and bracketed eaves, helped popularize the Italianate style in America. Woodrow Wilson lived here as university president; today it is the faculty club.

traditions.name: Founders' statues and footprints
traditions.description: Legend says the statues of Ezra Cornell and Andrew Dickson White will walk off their pedestals and shake hands on the Arts Quad under certain impossible conditions, and painted footprints between them mark the legend. Look for the footprints and pose between the two founders.

traditions.name: Cornell Chimes in McGraw Tower
traditions.description: Student chimesmasters play the 21-bell Cornell Chimes in McGraw Tower in three concerts a day during the academic year, and visitors are welcome at all of them. Listen from Ho Plaza or the Arts Quad.

traditions.name: Dragon Day
traditions.description: On the Friday before spring break, first-year architecture students parade a huge handmade dragon past Sibley Hall toward the Arts Quad. Visitors can line the route and watch it go by.

details.airportInfo: Ithaca's small airport is a few miles north of campus. Many visitors instead fly into Syracuse and drive about an hour south.
details.funFact: McGraw Tower, built as part of Uris Library in 1891, houses the Cornell Chimes, the first chimes housed and rung on an American college campus. They still play three times a day during term.
details.languageInfo: Students say 'Libe Slope' for the hillside that Uris Library overlooks.
details.transportationFact: Cornell's hilltop campus is spread out and steep in places, so comfortable shoes help. TCAT buses connect campus with downtown Ithaca.

buildings.name: Uris Library
buildings.description: Cornell's oldest library, opened in 1891 with McGraw Tower and its famous chimes rising beside it. Inside is the A. D. White Library, a 'library within a library' named for the university's first president.

buildings.name: Morrill Hall
buildings.description: Completed in 1866 and named for Senator Justin Morrill, author of the land-grant act that helped found the university, this hall was declared a National Historic Landmark in 1965.
buildings.architect: Harlow Wilcox and Cyrus K. Porter

buildings.name: A. D. White House
buildings.description: The richly carved stone mansion that Cornell's first president commissioned in 1871 as a home and a source of artistic inspiration for students. It was later the university art museum and now houses the Society for the Humanities.
buildings.architect: William Henry Miller and Charles Babcock

buildings.name: Willard Straight Hall
buildings.description: Cornell's student union, built of local bluestone and opened in 1925 as a memorial to Willard Straight. Its Gothic halls were the scene of the 1969 student protest that reshaped the university.

buildings.name: Bailey Hall
buildings.description: Cornell's largest auditorium is a Greek Revival amphitheatre of 1912, wrapped by a colonnaded portico with monumental stairs up to its main doors. Its acoustics were once praised as 'by God', its wooden seats less so.

traditions.name: Find the owl on Alma Mater
traditions.description: An owl, a symbol of wisdom, is hidden in the folds of Alma Mater's robe near her leg, and superstition says the first new student to find it becomes valedictorian. Visitors can hunt for the owl on the statue in front of Low Library.

traditions.name: Low Steps
traditions.description: The wide steps of Low Memorial Library, nicknamed 'Low Beach', are Columbia's favourite meeting spot. Sit on the steps and take in the view down to Butler Library.

traditions.name: The Sundial
traditions.description: The 1914 Class of 1885 Sundial at the centre of College Walk lost its granite ball in 1946, but its platform remains a classic gathering place and free-speech corner. It is also where the winter tree lighting and Yule Log ceremonies begin.

traditions.name: College Walk tree lighting
traditions.description: Each early December, the trees along College Walk are lit in a ceremony with a cappella music and hot chocolate, and the lights stay on until the end of February. Walk College Walk after dark in winter to see them.

details.airportInfo: LaGuardia is about 25 minutes by car from Morningside Heights. JFK and Newark are farther out but connect to the subway and trains into Manhattan.
details.funFact: Columbia's Morningside Heights campus was laid out by McKim, Mead & White in the 1890s around domed Low Memorial Library, whose steps hold Daniel Chester French's statue Alma Mater.
details.languageInfo: Low Memorial Library is simply 'Low' to students.
details.transportationFact: The campus is a compact grid of quads that is easy to walk. The 1 train's 116 Street–Columbia University station is right at the main gates on Broadway.

buildings.name: Low Memorial Library
buildings.description: Charles Follen McKim's domed, Greek-cross temple of learning sits at the head of a grand flight of steps, with Daniel Chester French's Alma Mater statue waiting halfway up. Built as the central library, it has held the university's administration since 1934.

buildings.name: Butler Library
buildings.description: Columbia's largest library faces Low across South Field, its façade inscribed with the names of great writers and thinkers. Built in 1931–1934, it stays at least partly open 24 hours a day during the academic year.

buildings.name: St. Paul's Chapel
buildings.description: Red brick and limestone outside, Byzantine within, under a dome of green glazed tiles 91 feet high. Built in 1903–1907, it was the first building on the campus not designed by McKim, Mead & White.

buildings.name: Philosophy Hall
buildings.description: One of McKim, Mead & White's original campus buildings, completed in 1910. It is a National Historic Landmark because Edwin Armstrong invented FM radio in its laboratories in the early 1930s.

buildings.name: Casa Italiana
buildings.description: Modelled on a 15th-century Roman palazzo, this 1927 building by William M. Kendall of McKim, Mead & White brings a slice of Renaissance Rome to Amsterdam Avenue. It houses the Italian Academy for Advanced Studies in America.

traditions.name: The Button
traditions.description: Claes Oldenburg's Split Button sits on College Green, and student lore says it is the button that popped off Benjamin Franklin's vest, rolled down Locust Walk and split in two. It is a central campus landmark and a popular photo stop.

traditions.name: Ivy Day stones on College Hall
traditions.description: Since 1873 each graduating class has set an engraved Ivy Stone into a campus building, and there are now nearly 200 around campus. Start at College Hall and look for the class-year stones in the walls.

traditions.name: Hey Day on Locust Walk
traditions.description: Each spring, juniors in straw-style hats march down Locust Walk to College Hall to be declared seniors, a tradition dating back to Class Day in 1865. Visitors can watch the procession pass along the walk.

details.airportInfo: PHL is about 15 minutes by car from campus. SEPTA's Airport Line train runs to University City station, next to the campus.
details.funFact: Penn's campus spans eras: Frank Furness's fiery red Victorian library, the first student union on any American campus, and Louis Kahn's breakthrough Richards Laboratories all sit within a short walk.
details.languageInfo: The university goes by 'Penn' or 'UPenn' for short.
details.transportationFact: University City is flat and easy to walk. SEPTA trolleys, buses and the Market–Frankford Line connect campus with Center City Philadelphia.

buildings.name: Fisher Fine Arts Library
buildings.description: Frank Furness's red sandstone, brick and terra-cotta giant, part fortress and part cathedral, opened in 1891 as Penn's main library. Today it is the fine arts library and a National Historic Landmark.

buildings.name: College Hall
buildings.description: The oldest building on Penn's West Philadelphia campus owes its distinctive green colour to serpentine stone. Its top floor was purpose-built for the Philomathean Society, which still meets there.

buildings.name: Houston Hall
buildings.description: Completed in 1896, this Collegiate Gothic hall was the first student union built on an American college campus, and it is still Penn's student union today.
buildings.architect: Frank Miles Day, William C. Hays and Milton Bennett Medary

buildings.name: Penn Museum
buildings.description: A campus landmark of courtyards, gardens, a reflecting pool and a dramatic rotunda, designed by a team of Penn's own architecture faculty. Only a third of the grand original plan was built, and it holds a 13-ton granite sphinx of Ramesses II.
buildings.architect: Wilson Eyre, Cope & Stewardson and Frank Miles Day

buildings.name: Richards Medical Research Laboratories
buildings.description: The building that made Louis Kahn's career: clusters of laboratory towers flanked by brick shafts for stairs and air ducts, inspired by the medieval towers of Italy. Its clear split between 'served' and 'servant' spaces set new directions for modern architecture.

traditions.name: Van Wickle Gates
traditions.description: The centre Van Wickle Gates open only for Convocation and Commencement, and superstition says a student who passes through them more than twice will not graduate. Visitors can see the 1901 wrought-iron gates on Prospect Street and walk through the side gates instead.

traditions.name: Bronze Bruno
traditions.description: A seven-foot bronze of Bruno, Brown's bear mascot, stands on the College Green on a pedestal holding a slate rock said to be one Roger Williams stepped on in 1636. Stop by for a photo with the mascot.

details.airportName: Rhode Island T. F. Green International Airport
details.airportInfo: T. F. Green is in Warwick, about 20 minutes south of College Hill. Boston Logan is roughly an hour and a half away by car or train.
details.funFact: University Hall, built in 1770, is one of only seven college buildings in the United States still standing from before the American Revolution.
details.languageInfo: Students call the John Hay Library simply 'the Hay'.
details.transportationFact: Brown sits on steep College Hill above downtown Providence and is easiest to explore on foot. RIPTA buses connect the hill with downtown and the train station.

buildings.name: University Hall
buildings.description: Brown's first building, raised in 1770 and once the largest building in Rhode Island. Framed by the Van Wickle Gates, this Georgian hall is called one of the icons of early American college architecture.
buildings.architect: Built by Nicholas Brown and Company

buildings.name: Sayles Hall
buildings.description: A rock-faced granite hall with brownstone trim, built in 1879–1881 in memory of a student who died young. Under its pine roof trusses sits the largest surviving Hutchings-Votey organ of its type, played at a midnight Halloween concert each year.

buildings.name: John Hay Library
buildings.description: Funded by Andrew Carnegie and named for his friend, Secretary of State John Hay, this white Vermont marble library opened in 1910 across from the Van Wickle Gates. It now keeps Brown's rare books, manuscripts and archives.

buildings.name: Rockefeller Library
buildings.description: Brown's main library, completed in 1964, is a bold Brutalist counterpoint to the marble John Hay Library across Prospect Street.

traditions.name: Dartmouth Night Bonfire
traditions.description: Each Homecoming weekend a large bonfire is built on the Green and first-year students run laps around it, one for each year of their class number. Visitors can watch the parade and the lit bonfire from around the Green.

traditions.name: Winter Carnival Snow Sculpture
traditions.description: Every February for Winter Carnival, students build a large themed snow sculpture on the Green. Visitors can stop by to see and photograph it.

traditions.name: Warner Bentley's Nose
traditions.description: Students rub the nose of the statue of Warner Bentley in the Hopkins Center for the Arts for good luck, which has left it discoloured. Visitors to the Hop can find the statue and give it a rub.

traditions.name: The Bema and the Old Pine
traditions.description: On Class Day seniors gather at the Bema, a natural amphitheatre in College Park, then walk up the hill to the stump of the Old Pine for a farewell ceremony that dates to the 1830s. Visitors can walk through College Park to see both spots.

details.airportInfo: Lebanon's small airport, just south of Hanover, has a few commuter flights. Most visitors fly into Boston Logan and drive about two hours north.
details.funFact: Baker Library's 200-foot tower, modelled on Philadelphia's Independence Hall, is the symbol of the college, and its basement holds José Clemente Orozco's fresco The Epic of American Civilization, a National Historic Landmark.
details.languageInfo: Students call the Hopkins Center for the Arts 'the Hop'.
details.transportationFact: Dartmouth's buildings ring the Green in the middle of Hanover, so everything is a short walk. Free Advance Transit buses link Hanover with nearby towns.

buildings.name: Baker-Berry Library
buildings.description: Jens Fredrick Larson modelled Baker Library and its 200-foot tower on Independence Hall; it opened in 1928. Downstairs, Orozco's fiery fresco cycle wraps the reserve corridor, and Robert Venturi's Berry Library was added alongside in 2000.
buildings.architect: Jens Fredrick Larson; Robert Venturi (Berry addition)

buildings.name: Hopkins Center for the Arts
buildings.description: Wallace Harrison's arched, glass-fronted arts center opened in 1962 and foreshadows his later design of the Metropolitan Opera House at Lincoln Center. It is the college's cultural hub.

buildings.name: Hood Museum of Art
buildings.description: Charles Moore and Chad Floyd's postmodern museum opened in 1985 for one of the oldest college art collections in America, begun in 1772. Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects added a new atrium and galleries in 2019.

buildings.name: Rauner Special Collections Library
buildings.description: Built in 1907 as Webster Hall, the college's main auditorium, this red-brick hall has a portico of four Corinthian limestone columns. Venturi, Scott Brown and Associates turned it into the special collections library in 1998.
buildings.architect: Charles A. Rich; Venturi, Scott Brown and Associates (conversion)

traditions.name: Healy Hall Seal
traditions.description: A mosaic Georgetown seal is set into the ground at the central entrance to Healy Hall, and students walk around it because legend says stepping on it means you won't graduate. Visitors can see the seal and watch students sidestep it.

traditions.name: The Exorcist Steps
traditions.description: The steep stone staircase from Prospect Street down to M Street appears in the final scene of The Exorcist, written by alumnus William Peter Blatty, and Hoyas make a point of running up them. Visitors can climb the public steps and take a photo.

details.airportInfo: Reagan National is about 15 minutes' drive from campus across the Potomac. Dulles International is farther out, roughly 45 minutes away.
details.funFact: Healy Hall, the spired landmark visible across the Potomac, was designed by Paul Pelz and John Smithmeyer, the same pair who designed the Library of Congress's Thomas Jefferson Building.
details.transportationFact: Georgetown has no Metro station of its own, so the university's free GUTS shuttle buses link campus with nearby Metro stops. The hilltop campus itself is easy to walk.

buildings.name: Healy Hall
buildings.description: Georgetown's flagship building, built in 1877–1879 by the architects of the Library of Congress's Jefferson Building. Inside are the elaborate Gaston Hall and Riggs Library, one of the few cast-iron libraries left in the country.
buildings.architect: John L. Smithmeyer and Paul J. Pelz

buildings.name: Old North
buildings.description: The oldest academic building on campus, completed in 1795 and one of the grandest buildings in Washington at the time. It was the university's flagship until Healy Hall and now houses the McCourt School of Public Policy.

buildings.name: Georgetown University Astronomical Observatory
buildings.description: Father James Curley planned this Greek Revival observatory and supervised its construction, finished in 1844. In 1846 it was used to fix the latitude and longitude of Washington, D.C.

buildings.name: Lauinger Library
buildings.description: John Carl Warnecke's Brutalist main library opened in 1970, designed as a modern interpretation of neighbouring Healy Hall, with a spire echoing Healy's clock tower. It holds 1.7 million volumes on six floors.
